title: A global Microsoft 365 outage has hit millions – what happened and when will it be fixed?
text:
A global outage has hit Microsoft 365. The company has not indicated why the outage has lasted so long, but ruled out a cyber-attack as the cause. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images
A global outage has hit Microsoft 365. The company has not indicated why the outage has lasted so long, but ruled out a cyber-attack as the cause. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images
Millions of people were unable to access their emails, Teams chats or meetings on Thursday night and Friday morning after a Microsoft 365 outage brought down services across the globe.
The incident affected businesses, government agencies and even Microsoft employees. Businesses, government agencies and vital services around the world have all reported issues, from the US House of Representatives to an Australian spy agency and airlines in India. In the UK, police services, ambulances and hospitals reported issues with email services and online form submissions.
The outage has affected millions but is also patchy; some users are still able to access some aspects of Microsoft’s service, and service is resuming in some parts of the world faster than others. Microsoft and independent internet researchers have reported incremental improvements in service during Friday.
Experts say that the outage has laid bare the dangerous dependence of countries such as the UK on a few US tech companies.
What happened and why – and what does it say about online services in 2026?
What happened with Microsoft?
At about 6pm GMT on Thursday, the outage website Down Detector showed an increase in users reporting issues with Microsoft 365, the suite of cloud software that includes Teams, Word Excel, PowerPoint and Outlook.
The outage has lasted for more than 19 hours at the time of reporting, with Microsoft working to bring services back.
By Friday morning, Microsoft had narrowed down most of the problems to Microsoft Exchange, the email service behind Outlook. Teams meetings and chats had returned to service.
By midday UK time, Microsoft said there was “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”, improvements in North America and Asia Pacific, and Japan was “stable”.
What caused the Microsoft outage?
So far, the problem appears to be a configuration update that resulted in some servers becoming overloaded and taken offline, Microsoft indicated.
When the company attempted to apply a fix, servers that had come back online again became unresponsive when traffic began returning to them.
As some servers went down, traffic was funnelled on to the remaining servers, causing traffic problems for those remaining online.
To understand what was bringing down the servers, the company began limiting the traffic that could reach affected servers in specific locations, and on some servers rolled back to an earlier software configuration to see if it fixed the problem.
Why has Microsoft 365 been down for so long?
An outage that runs for so long for a service as critical as Microsoft 365 is unusual. The company has not said why it has lasted this long, but a clue might be in its updates: as servers returned to being unresponsive after being fixed, engineers had to work through alternative solutions, taking longer than expected to get servers back up and running.
Who was affected by the Microsoft outage?
In the UK, police services, the Bank of England, vital health services – such as ambulances and the NHS – and schools have been affected. In Australia, many people who rely on Microsoft 365 were reporting being unable to access their inboxes, including in councils, state and federal government agencies, courts and schools.
Across Europe, government agencies in the Netherlands, Belgium, Germany and France reported issues, with a French municipality instructing residents to phone instead in case of need.
In Japan, government services and private companies were widely affected, with some employees saying they were switching back to sending faxes. The shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and railway stations, while Taisho, a big pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
The UK government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on government services, adding that there were “robust contingency plans in place to minimise disruption”.
The NHS, which in England has a five-year deal to use Microsoft 365, said that a range of services have been disrupted.
The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted.
In financial markets, some portfolio managers have been unable to use email to authenticate their access to some trading platforms.
Was the Microsoft outage a cyber-attack?
Given the recent OpenAI agent attack on Medicare, and the spate of cyber-attacks in Europe bringing down internet-connected fridges, some quickly guessed the global outage might be a new attack on critical infrastructure. Microsoft quickly hosed down the idea, saying there was no indication it was a cyber-attack. There is also no indication presently that it came from AI, although AI tools have been fingered as a source of other high-profile recent outages.
What does the incident say about our reliance in online services?
UK politicians and experts have said that outages such as this underscore the world’s reliance on cloud services provided by a few massive US tech companies – Amazon, Google and Microsoft. This reliance has been a growing source of unease through each high profile outage. It has grown more pronounced because of the hostility of the Trump administration towards Europe, which has prompted some governments to consider alternatives to its software.
As the name Microsoft 365 implies, the world has quickly become accustomed to online services being available 24/7. Given software is no longer solely downloaded to individual PCs but is also stored on a server owned by a company, outages such as this will happen. Most of the time they are brief but sometimes they are not.
There are many different pieces of the puzzle keeping services online – but the effect of one of those services going down is much greater than it ever has been.
An associate professor at Australia’s RMIT University, Mark Gregory, said it was important for organisations to thoroughly test updates before rolling them out to the live network. That is in addition to the extra security testing companies must carry out to ensure their services are protected from threat actors armed with AI tools that can find vulnerabilities quicker than ever before.
Should we have backup options when services go down?
Gregory said companies that rely on services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options such as Google’s Gmail in the event of an outage.
Others have suggested the free and open-source Office alternative, LibreOffice.
